analysis.one_liner: Gives the consumer financial watchdog power to enforce protections owed to active-duty servicemembers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in July 2017 with 10 Democratic cosponsors, never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the House Financial Services Committee before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill changes the 2010 consumer financial protection law so that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — the federal agency that polices lending and financial products — can supervise and enforce protections that service members already have under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. Those include the 6% interest-rate cap on debts incurred before military service, protection from being served with default judgments while deployed, eviction protections, limits on repossession, motor-vehicle lease termination rights, and the right to cancel a cellphone contract during a deployment. The bill does not create new rights; it adds an enforcement cop.
analysis.who_benefits: Active-duty servicemembers and their families. Today the Justice Department enforces the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act largely case by case, after a violation has happened. This bill would have let the CFPB examine lenders, mortgage servicers, auto-leasing companies, and phone carriers for SCRA violations in advance, and enforce rules like the 6% interest-rate cap on pre-service debts, eviction protections, protection from default judgments, motor-vehicle lease termination, and cellphone contract cancellation during deployment.

how_it_helps.text: Adds servicemembers covered by specified sections of the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's definition of 'covered persons', giving the bureau oversight and protection authority over them [S2, S3].

Covers specific SCRA protections: interest rates on pre-service debts, default judgments, evictions, installment contracts, mortgages, motor vehicle leases, telephone service contracts, and rights of reserves ordered to active duty — while excluding insurance, bailments, and child custody proceedings [S2, S3].

The change would let the CFPB proactively supervise financial firms rather than leaving enforcement of servicemember protections solely to after-the-fact lawsuits by the Justice Department or individual troops.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer lenders, mortgage servicers and foreclosure firms, auto-leasing and finance companies, debt collectors who obtain default judgments against deployed troops, and telecom carriers. They would face CFPB examinations and penalties for SCRA violations, and pass some compliance costs to all customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lenders, servicers, auto lessors, and telecoms

drawbacks.text: The bill creates no new substantive rights; it only gives the CFPB authority over protections that already exist under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act and are already enforceable by the Justice Department and the courts [S2, S3].

Extending CFPB supervision to SCRA-covered transactions would add compliance costs for lenders, servicers, leasing companies, and landlords — some of them small businesses — costs that could be passed on to customers in the form of higher rates or fees. Supporters of a narrower CFPB also argued at the time that the bureau's enforcement authority should not reach areas the Justice Department already polices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a modest, targeted bill: it added no new entitlement and no spending, only an enforcement cop for protections Congress had already written for troops. The real cost falls on financial firms that would face supervision and penalties, and some of that cost would reach consumers as compliance expense. The added benefit to servicemembers is real but bounded — it strengthens enforcement of existing rules rather than closing gaps in them. An honest supporter would acknowledge it is a second-best tool that leaves the underlying protections unchanged.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced in July 2017 and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA) introduced the Military Consumer Protection Act on July 24, 2017, joined by 10 original cosponsors including Reps. Walz, Heck, Velazquez, Sherman, Meeks, Green, Kildee, Beatty, Gonzalez, and Lynch [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day it was introduced [S5].

The bill amends the definition of 'covered persons' under the Consumer Financial Protection Act to add persons protected by sections 101, 106, 107, 108, 201, 207, 301, 302, 303, 305, and 305A of the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, with carve-outs for insurance, bailments, and child custody [S3].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded for the bill; the complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer finance firms — lenders, mortgage servicers, auto-leasing companies, debt collectors, and telecom carriers — are better off, because their dealings with servicemembers remained outside Consumer Financial Protection Bureau oversight for the rest of the Congress. The committee leadership that declined to act also avoided a vote on a bill its majority did not support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumer finance firms that escaped oversight

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.role: U.S. Representative (CA), sponsor; ranking Democrat on the Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Military Consumer Protection Act on July 24, 2017.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the complete action history records no action beyond the referral.

against.name: Rep. Jeb Hensarling
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral throughout the 115th Congress, never brought the bill to a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the record shows no roll-call split; all 10 cosponsors were Democrats, the sponsor was the committee's top Democrat, and the Republican-majority committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: SCRA enforcement targets charging active-duty troops above the 6% interest-rate cap on pre-service debts and wrongful foreclosures and evictions. CFPB supervision would have exposed these firms to examinations and penalties for practices that currently draw consequences mainly through slow Justice Department lawsuits.

The bill covers the SCRA's motor-vehicle lease protections, including servicemembers' right to terminate a lease without penalty after a deployment order. Firms that profit from lease breakage fees would have faced CFPB enforcement.

SCRA default-judgment provisions protect deployed troops from being sued and losing by default without notice. CFPB oversight would have added a check on a practice that garnishes wages and seizes property from absent servicemembers.

The bill covers the SCRA provision allowing troops to cancel telephone service contracts upon deployment orders without early-termination fees. Carriers would have faced CFPB supervision over these cancellation rights.
